title: When I dance, I dance
hook: when I dance, I dance; when I sleep, I sleep (Essays 3.13)

segments.voice: Yesterday, plague years, and your line was the peasants' calm. Did you think of one plain, brave person and thank them? A new week starts now. Day one thousand one hundred seventy.

Dinner is on the table, the phone is next to the plate, the news is murmuring in the other room, and half your mind is already in tomorrow's meeting. Afterward, you could hardly say what you ate. Montaigne, in the last essay of his book, called Of experience, describes a different way of being at the table, and on the dance floor, and in bed at night. The sentence could hardly be plainer: when I dance, I dance; when I sleep, I sleep.
screen: `DINNER, PHONE, NEWS, TOMORROW.` → `WHAT DID YOU EAT?` → `WHEN I DANCE, I DANCE.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence. It sounds almost too obvious. Of course when you dance, you dance. But Montaigne means it as a discipline: when he does a thing, he tries to be wholly in it, not half there and half somewhere else. Second, the orchard. He doesn't pretend to be perfect at this. When he walks alone in a beautiful orchard, he says, his thoughts sometimes drift off to far-away matters for part of the time. And for the other part, he brings them back: to the walk, to the orchard, to the sweetness of being alone there, and to himself. Drift, and return. That's the whole skill. Third, the body's ordinary work. In the same essay he says nature has made the actions it requires of us pleasant: eating, sleeping, resting. To rush them, or to look down on them as beneath a serious mind, is to miss something nature gave us on purpose. He's suspicious of people who treat a good meal as a waste of time. Fourth, the great men. Montaigne points out that even generals and rulers he admired found time to enjoy ordinary pleasures in the middle of great affairs. Being wholly present wasn't a distraction from serious life; it was part of living it well. Nobody needs a dance floor for this. Washing a cup, walking to the car, hugging a child at the door. When you wash, wash. When you hug, hug. And when your mind wanders off, bring it back to the orchard.
screen: `DO ONE THING WHOLLY.` · `DRIFT, THEN COME BACK.` · `NATURE MADE NEEDS PLEASANT.` · `PRESENT IN GREAT AFFAIRS TOO.` · then, large: `WHEN I DANCE, I DANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing wholly, and the thing is breathing. Sit. When you breathe in, breathe in. When you breathe out, breathe out. That's all. Your mind will wander, the way Montaigne's did in the orchard. When you notice it has gone somewhere else, don't scold it. Just bring it back: to the breath, to the chair, to this room, to yourself. Drift and return, as many times as it takes. The bell holds the time.
When I dance. Montaigne's short rule for being wholly in what you're doing, and coming back when you drift. Today's word.
Your line: when I dance, I dance. Today, pick one ordinary act, a meal, a walk, a shower, and do only that, start to finish. Day one thousand one hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often quote his line from Of experience, when I dance, I dance; when I sleep, I sleep, as a picture of giving full attention to ordinary acts.

myth: Montaigne claims his mind never wanders
in the orchard his thoughts drift for part of the time, and he brings them back.
he says nature made the actions it requires of us pleasant
eating, sleeping and resting are given to us to enjoy, not rush.
he says serious people should skip pleasures to save time
he's suspicious of that, and notes great men who enjoyed ordinary pleasures amid great affairs.

fork.setup: you're walking in a lovely orchard, like Montaigne, and your mind drifts to tomorrow's problems. what does he do?
options: give up on the walk and go solve the problems.
let them drift for a while, then bring them back to the orchard.
force himself never to think of anything else.
fork.reveal: he admits his thoughts wander part of the time; the other part, he brings them back to the walk and to himself.

trapdoor: what you thought: when I dance, I dance is just a nice saying about enjoying parties.
what it means: it's a discipline of being wholly in each act, and returning when the mind drifts.
what a scholar hears: it comes from Of experience, the essay that closes Montaigne's book, where he praises the body's ordinary pleasures.
